name: Why did humans switch from hunting to farming?
short: Because the end of the Ice Age made wild cereals abundant and climate stable, people settled near them, their numbers grew, and once they had grown they could no longer go back.
how: Around 11,700 years ago, the Ice Age ended and the climate became warmer and more stable. In the Fertile Crescent, people such as the Natufians were already harvesting wild wheat and barley and living in permanent villages. By replanting seeds from the plants that did not scatter their grain, they unknowingly bred domestic crops; wild goats, sheep, pigs and cattle were tamed soon after. Farming arose independently in at least 7–11 places: China (rice and millet), New Guinea (taro, bananas), Mesoamerica (maize), the Andes (potatoes), Africa (sorghum) and India (rice, millets).
why: Farming produced far more food per acre, so populations grew, and larger groups pushed hunters out. Once villages had grown, nobody could return to foraging without famine.
theories: Jared Diamond called farming 'the worst mistake in the history of the human race': early farmers were shorter, had worse teeth, more disease and more work than hunter-gatherers. Other theories stress feasting and religion — Göbekli Tepe's monumental temples were built by hunters before farming, so gathering for ritual may have encouraged cultivation; others propose a population squeeze or the Younger Dryas cold snap.
reshaped: Farming created surplus, property, inheritance, social classes, armies, kings, writing and cities — and also epidemic diseases from animals, patriarchy and slavery. Almost everything in recorded history follows from it.
connections: Neolithic Revolution; Göbekli Tepe; Çatalhöyük; Mehrgarh; Fertile Crescent; Dog domestication; Maize domestication

name: How did the first towns and cities form?
short: Farming villages grew around fertile river valleys; surplus food let specialists, priests and rulers live in central places, which drew in trade and people.
how: Early towns like Jericho (c. 9000 BCE) and Çatalhöyük (c. 7000 BCE) had thousands of people but no palaces. True cities appeared in Mesopotamia: Uruk reached 40,000 people around 3200 BCE, with temples, administrators and full-time craftsmen. The Indus cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro had planned grids and drains; Egypt, China, Mesoamerica and the Andes developed their own cities independently.
why: Irrigation farming in river valleys produced huge surpluses but needed coordination. Temples stored grain, traders gathered, defence was easier with walls, and cities offered opportunity.
theories: Older 'hydraulic' theories (Karl Wittfogel) said irrigation created despotic states; newer evidence (David Graeber and David Wengrow's The Dawn of Everything) shows some early cities, such as those of the Indus or Ukraine's Trypillia mega-sites, were surprisingly egalitarian.
reshaped: Cities created writing, specialised jobs, monumental architecture, laws and bureaucracy — and the word 'civilisation' itself comes from the Latin for city-dweller.
connections: Uruk, the first city; Mohenjo-daro; Dholavira; Çatalhöyük; Sumer; Indus Valley Civilisation; Invention of writing

name: How did bands become tribes, chiefdoms and states?
short: As populations grew, small equal bands gave way to larger groups held together first by kinship and ritual, then by chiefs who redistributed food, and finally by kings with armies, taxes and laws.
how: Hunter-gatherer bands of 20–50 shared food and avoided bosses. Farming tribes of hundreds organised by clan and lineage; chiefdoms of thousands, like those of Polynesia or Bronze Age Europe, had hereditary chiefs who controlled surplus and gave feasts. States, like Sumer or Egypt, had kings, professional soldiers, tax collectors and priests.
why: Groups needed to resolve disputes between strangers, defend stored food, and organise large projects. Those who controlled surplus or weapons turned influence into permanent power.
theories: Anthropologist Elman Service proposed the band–tribe–chiefdom–state sequence; Robert Carneiro argued states formed through warfare in 'circumscribed' areas where people could not escape; James C. Scott (Against the Grain) argues early states were built on grain taxes and forced labour, and many people fled them. Robin Dunbar suggested humans can maintain only about 150 real relationships, so larger groups needed shared myths, gods or flags.
reshaped: States brought order, laws and great works, but also slavery, taxes and war on a new scale.
connections: Sumer; Ancient Egypt; Code of Hammurabi; Mahajanapadas

name: Why did organised religion arise?
short: Belief in spirits seems natural to the human mind; as societies grew large, organised religions with moral gods helped strangers trust each other, and gave rulers legitimacy.
how: Burials with grave goods (over 100,000 years ago) suggest belief in an afterlife; cave art and Göbekli Tepe suggest ritual. Early cities built temples to city gods; Egyptian pharaohs and Mesopotamian kings claimed divine favour. In the 'Axial Age' (c. 800–200 BCE) the Buddha, Mahavira, the Upanishads, Confucius, Laozi, the Hebrew prophets and Greek philosophers shifted religion toward ethics and personal salvation.
why: Psychologists find humans naturally see agents and purpose in events. Shared rituals bind groups, and believing a god watches makes people more honest.
theories: Ara Norenzayan's 'Big Gods' theory says moralising gods enabled large societies; a 2019 Nature study argued the opposite — big gods appeared after societies grew; Marx called religion the 'opium of the people'; Durkheim said it was society worshipping itself.
reshaped: Religion shaped laws, art, architecture, wars and morality, and remains central to most people's lives.
connections: Göbekli Tepe; Hinduism; Buddhism; Judaism; Christianity; Islam; Akhenaten's religious revolution

name: Why was writing invented?
short: For accounting: temple administrators in Sumer needed to record grain, beer and livestock; poetry and law came later.
how: Clay tokens for counting goods evolved into marks on tablets in Uruk around 3200 BCE; cuneiform developed over centuries. Writing was independently invented in Egypt, China (oracle bones, c. 1200 BCE) and Mesoamerica. The Indus script remains undeciphered. The alphabet was invented around 1800 BCE by Semitic workers in Egypt.
why: Bureaucracy, trade and taxation needed records beyond human memory.
theories: Denise Schmandt-Besserat's token theory is widely accepted for Mesopotamia; Chinese writing may have begun with divination.
reshaped: Writing created history, law codes, literature, science and religious scriptures — and the power of literate elites.
connections: Invention of writing; Sumer; Cuneiform; Indus script; Egyptian hieroglyphs; Phoenician alphabet

name: Why was money invented?
short: To make trade, taxes and payments easier than barter; but debts and credit came before coins.
how: Mesopotamians used silver weights and barley as money and recorded debts on clay. The first coins were struck in Lydia (Turkey) around 600 BCE from electrum; punch-marked coins appeared in India's Mahajanapadas and spade coins in China around the same time. China invented paper money in the Song dynasty (11th century).
why: States needed to pay soldiers and collect taxes; markets needed a common measure.
theories: Economists long assumed money grew out of barter; anthropologists like David Graeber found no society that ran on barter and argued debt and credit came first.
reshaped: Money allowed empires, banks, trade networks and capitalism.
connections: Lydia; Mahajanapadas; Song dynasty; Silk Road

name: Why do empires rise and fall?
short: Empires rise through military advantage, wealth and organisation; they fall when costs outgrow revenues, elites split, climate or disease strike, or outsiders exploit weakness.
how: Rome, the Han, the Mauryas, the Abbasids, the Mughals and the British all followed patterns of expansion, peak and decline lasting a few centuries.
why: Ibn Khaldun (1377) said empires are founded by tough groups bound by solidarity (asabiyyah), which fades with luxury after three or four generations.
theories: Edward Gibbon blamed Christianity and barbarism for Rome's fall; Joseph Tainter blames rising complexity; Peter Turchin blames elite overproduction; Kyle Harper stresses plague and climate; Paul Kennedy argued 'imperial overstretch'.
reshaped: The rise and fall of empires drew the map of today's nations, languages and religions.
connections: Roman Empire; Fall of the Western Roman Empire; Maurya Empire; Mughal Empire; British Empire; Ibn Khaldun

name: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain?
short: Britain combined cheap coal, expensive labour, secure property rights, a big colonial market and a culture of tinkering, so it paid to invent machines.
how: Textile machines like the spinning jenny and water frame, then James Watt's improved steam engine (1769), moved production into factories. Coal powered iron and railways; by 1850 Britain was the 'workshop of the world'.
why: Robert Allen argues British wages were high and coal cheap, making machines profitable there first. Others point to the Glorious Revolution protecting property, the Royal Society, patents, and profits from slavery and colonies, including India's textile market.
theories: Kenneth Pomeranz's 'Great Divergence' argues China's Yangzi delta was as advanced until 1800; Britain's luck was coal near the surface and American colonies. Indian historians stress that British tariffs and colonial policy destroyed India's textile industry.
reshaped: Industrialisation created the modern world: cities, the working class, socialism, mass consumption, global empire and climate change.
connections: Industrial Revolution; Watt's steam engine; British Raj; Glorious Revolution; Atlantic slave trade; Luddites

name: Why do revolutions happen?
short: When a government is broke or humiliated, its elites are divided, and ordinary people are angry about prices or injustice, an old regime can collapse; new ideas then decide what replaces it.
how: The American, French, Haitian, Russian, Chinese and Iranian revolutions overthrew governments; each began with a state crisis (debt, war or famine), mass protest, and then struggle among revolutionaries.
why: Theda Skocpol argued revolutions come when states break down from foreign pressure and peasants revolt. James Davies said they happen when rising expectations are suddenly dashed.
theories: Marxists see revolutions as class struggle; Crane Brinton found a pattern in which moderates give way to radicals, terror and finally a strongman (Napoleon, Stalin). Recent scholars stress social media and urban protest.
reshaped: Revolutions spread democracy, nationalism, socialism and human rights, but also terror and dictatorship.
connections: French Revolution; American Revolution; Haitian Revolution; Russian Revolution; Chinese Revolution; Iranian Revolution; Revolutions of 1848; Age of Revolutions

name: Why do rebellions break out?
short: Rebellions break out when grievances such as taxes, land loss or religious insult meet a spark and leaders who can organise.
how: Spartacus's slave revolt, the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, the Taiping Rebellion, the Santhal rebellion and the 1857 rebellion all started with local grievances that spread.
why: Rebellions usually follow new taxes, famine, foreign rule or religious threats; the greased-cartridge rumour of 1857 was the spark for anger over annexations and land revenue.
theories: James C. Scott wrote of 'everyday resistance' and the 'moral economy' of peasants; others stress military failure of states.
reshaped: Most rebellions failed, but they forced reforms, as when the British Crown took over India from the Company after 1857.
connections: Indian Rebellion of 1857; Taiping Rebellion; Spartacus revolt; Peasants' Revolt; Santhal rebellion; Yellow Turban rebellion

name: Why did Europe colonise most of the world?
short: A mix of geography, competition between states, ocean-going ships and guns, joint-stock companies, and epidemics that killed most native Americans.
how: From 1492 Spain and Portugal, then the Dutch, British and French, built sea empires. By 1914 Europeans controlled about 84% of the world's land.
why: Constant war between European states drove military innovation; trading companies raised money from investors; and smallpox and other diseases killed perhaps 90% of the native population of the Americas.
theories: Jared Diamond's Guns, Germs and Steel points to geography; Kenneth Pomeranz to coal and colonies; Philip Hoffman to gunpowder tournament competition; others stress Asian empires' internal crises.
reshaped: Colonialism shaped borders, languages, races, economies and inequality across the world.
connections: Age of Discovery; Columbian exchange; East India Company rule; Scramble for Africa; Atlantic slave trade

name: Why did the Bronze Age collapse?
short: A 'perfect storm': drought, earthquakes, rebellions, broken trade networks and raids by the Sea Peoples brought down interconnected palace kingdoms.
how: In a few decades the Hittite Empire, Mycenaean Greece, Ugarit and many Levantine cities were destroyed; Egypt survived, weakened. Writing disappeared from Greece for 400 years.
why: Palace economies depended on long-distance trade in copper and tin; when trade failed, so did they.
theories: Eric Cline (1177 BC) argues systems collapse; pollen data show severe drought.
reshaped: Out of the collapse came the Iron Age, the Phoenician alphabet, Israel and classical Greece.
connections: Sea Peoples' raids; Hittites; Mycenaean Greece; Phoenician alphabet

name: How did the Black Death change the world?
short: By killing a third to half of Europe, it made labour scarce, raised wages, weakened feudalism and the Church, and pushed Europe toward new ideas.
how: Plague spread along trade routes from Central Asia; in Europe it killed about 25–50 million people.
why: Surviving peasants demanded higher wages; landlords' attempts to freeze them sparked revolts like the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.
theories: Historians debate whether it caused the Renaissance; it certainly brought persecution of Jews, blamed for poisoning wells.
reshaped: Labour-saving inventions, wage labour, and doubts about the Church followed.
connections: Black Death; Peasants' Revolt; Mongol Empire; Renaissance; Protestant Reformation

name: Why did nations and nationalism appear?
short: Printing, mass schooling, newspapers and revolutions taught millions of strangers to imagine themselves as one people sharing a language, history and destiny.
how: The French Revolution created the idea of the sovereign nation; Germany and Italy unified in the 1860s–70s; anti-colonial movements built India and others.
why: Benedict Anderson called nations 'imagined communities' created by print capitalism.
theories: Ernest Gellner linked nationalism to industrial society; Anthony Smith stressed older ethnic roots.
reshaped: Nationalism created most modern states — and fuelled world wars and genocide.
connections: French Revolution; Indian independence movement; World War I; Revolutions of 1848

name: Why did slavery exist and why was it abolished?
short: Slavery existed wherever labour was valuable and people could be captured; it ended through slave resistance, religious and Enlightenment campaigns, and economic change.
how: The Atlantic slave trade carried about 12.5 million Africans to the Americas. Haiti's revolution (1791–1804) and abolitionists in Britain led to the British ban of the slave trade (1807) and of slavery (1833); the US ended it with the Civil War (1865).
why: Eric Williams argued slavery was abolished when it stopped being profitable; others stress moral campaigns and resistance.
theories: Debates continue about how much slavery funded industrialisation.
reshaped: Abolition changed economies, sent indentured Indian labourers across the world, and left legacies of racism.
connections: Atlantic slave trade; Haitian Revolution; Abolition of slavery in the British Empire; American Civil War
